sourceNote: Selective DGT editorial notes for James.

1:2: πειρασμοί can mean trials or temptations. Here the context is external testing, so DGT uses “trials”; the same word-group shifts toward temptation in verses 13–14.
1:6: διακρινόμενος can mean doubting, wavering, or being divided. DGT uses “doubting” here, while verse 8 makes the dividedness explicit with “double-minded.”
1:17: “Father of lights” is James’s own expression. DGT retains it rather than paraphrasing “Creator of the heavenly lights.”
2:14: The Greek question uses ἡ πίστις with the article: “Can the faith save him?” In context it refers to the kind of claimed faith just described, not a blanket denial that faith saves.
2:24: James says a person is “justified by works and not by faith alone.” DGT keeps δικαιοῦται as “is justified” and leaves the theological relationship to Paul to interpretation rather than harmonizing the wording.
3:6: “The course of life” renders τὸν τροχὸν τῆς γενέσεως, literally something like “the wheel/cycle of existence.” DGT uses an idiomatic phrase while retaining the image of the tongue setting the whole course ablaze.
4:5: James 4:5 is notoriously difficult syntactically, and the wording does not correspond exactly to a known Old Testament quotation. DGT follows the displayed Greek closely and avoids supplying an unidentified source.
5:4: “Lord of Hosts” renders Κύριος Σαβαώθ, retaining the Semitic divine title rather than replacing it with “Lord Almighty.”
5:15: σώσει can mean save, rescue, or make well. In the immediate setting of sickness DGT keeps “save,” while the following verb “raise up” also contributes to the healing context.
5:20: The pronoun in “save a soul from death” is not explicit enough in Greek to force whether it is the wanderer’s soul or the restorer’s; DGT leaves the referent unstated.
